column37: Overall risk of bias was judged High because weaknesses in the randomization process and post-randomization handling of participants are likely to have distorted the comparison: matched pairs were randomized by the statistician using random number tables, yet aspects of trial conduct (e.g., blood-count verification and delayed infusions in 4 cladribine and 2 placebo patients) could have made allocation predictable, and two cladribine-assigned participants lost to follow-up were replaced without replacing their placebo counterparts. In addition, deviations from intended intervention occurred—dose intensity and number of courses varied (one patient received five courses before dose reduction; one received only two; two received three due to thrombocytopenia)—and these differences were not accounted for in the analysis. Missing data were handled asymmetrically (“the analyses… exclude the three cladribine patients who did not complete a full year”), introducing attrition/per-protocol bias. Although outcome assessment was blinded in a two-physician model and there were no specific concerns about selective reporting, the combined issues in randomization, deviations, and missing outcome data indicate a high overall risk of bias.

column37: Overall risk of bias was judged High because weaknesses in the randomization process and post-randomization handling of participants are likely to have distorted the comparison: matched pairs were randomized by the statistician using random number tables, yet aspects of trial conduct (e.g., blood-count verification and delayed infusions in 4 cladribine and 2 placebo patients) could have made allocation predictable, and two cladribine-assigned participants lost to follow-up were replaced without replacing their placebo counterparts. In addition, deviations from intended intervention occurred—dose intensity and number of courses varied (one patient received five courses before dose reduction; one received only two; two received three due to thrombocytopenia)—and these differences were not accounted for in the analysis. Missing data were handled asymmetrically (“the analyses… exclude the three cladribine patients who did not complete a full year”), introducing attrition/per-protocol bias. Although outcome assessment was blinded in a two-physician model and there were no specific concerns about selective reporting, the combined issues in randomization, deviations, and missing outcome data indicate a high overall risk of bias.

column37: Overall risk of bias was judged High because weaknesses in the randomization process and post-randomization handling of participants are likely to have distorted the comparison: matched pairs were randomized by the statistician using random number tables, yet aspects of trial conduct (e.g., blood-count verification and delayed infusions in 4 cladribine and 2 placebo patients) could have made allocation predictable, and two cladribine-assigned participants lost to follow-up were replaced without replacing their placebo counterparts. In addition, deviations from intended intervention occurred—dose intensity and number of courses varied (one patient received five courses before dose reduction; one received only two; two received three due to thrombocytopenia)—and these differences were not accounted for in the analysis. Missing data were handled asymmetrically (“the analyses… exclude the three cladribine patients who did not complete a full year”), introducing attrition/per-protocol bias. Although outcome assessment was blinded in a two-physician model and there were no specific concerns about selective reporting, the combined issues in randomization, deviations, and missing outcome data indicate a high overall risk of bias.

column37: Overall risk of bias was judged High because weaknesses in the randomization process and post-randomization handling of participants are likely to have distorted the comparison: matched pairs were randomized by the statistician using random number tables, yet aspects of trial conduct (e.g., blood-count verification and delayed infusions in 4 cladribine and 2 placebo patients) could have made allocation predictable, and two cladribine-assigned participants lost to follow-up were replaced without replacing their placebo counterparts. In addition, deviations from intended intervention occurred—dose intensity and number of courses varied (one patient received five courses before dose reduction; one received only two; two received three due to thrombocytopenia)—and these differences were not accounted for in the analysis. Missing data were handled asymmetrically (“the analyses… exclude the three cladribine patients who did not complete a full year”), introducing attrition/per-protocol bias. Although outcome assessment was blinded in a two-physician model and there were no specific concerns about selective reporting, the combined issues in randomization, deviations, and missing outcome data indicate a high overall risk of bias.

column29: As a Phase IV observational study, both participants and treating physicians were unblinded to treatment allocation. In CLASSIC-MS, follow-up cohorts were defined by actual exposure—“cladribine-exposed” versus “never-exposed”—rather than by the original randomized assignment. Because crossover occurred in the parent studies and only those who enrolled in CLASSIC-MS were analyzed roughly 10.9 years after the parent trials, the effect estimated is as-treated rather than the effect of assignment. These design features, together with post-randomization selection, create potential for a substantial impact on the relapse outcome when participants are analyzed in exposure-defined groups rather than according to their original assignment.
column31: Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants because CLASSIC-MS included only a subset of the parent CLARITY/Extension population who returned for a single long-term assessment ~10.9 years after the last parent-study dose. Inclusion required surviving to and consenting at the long-term visit, and relapse history or health status could plausibly influence participation; relapse information was also collected retrospectively at Study Visit 1, increasing the chance that missingness depended on the true relapse status. Moreover, follow-up cohorts were defined by exposure (“cladribine-exposed” vs “never-exposed”) rather than original randomized assignment, reinforcing post-randomization selection concerns; there is no evidence of analytic corrections or sensitivity analyses addressing bias from missing outcome data.
column33: Relapses were ascertained retrospectively from medical records and/or at the single long-term Study Visit 1 using conventional clinical criteria, which is an appropriate and sufficiently sensitive measurement approach (4.1), and the same ascertainment procedure appears to have been applied across exposure groups (4.2). Because determining whether an event qualifies as a relapse involves clinical judgement based on retrospective symptom reconstruction, such awareness could plausibly influence the classification of borderline events (4.4), and—given the unblinded setting and retrospective ascertainment—it is likely that knowledge of intervention status influenced outcome assessment to some extent (4.5).

column29: The treating physicians were blinded to treatment, and the study was conducted as double-blind. Nevertheless, treatment allocation was known at the analysis/reporting stage, as the authors were aware of the treatment groups from CLARITY. In the Extension, there were five arms; participants who had received placebo in CLARITY were directly assigned to cladribine 3.5 mg/kg without re-randomization. column31: In this study, approximately 7–11% of participants did not complete the observation period; fewer than 10% discontinued for ‘other’ reasons that were not further specified. However, among those randomized in CLARITY who subsequently enrolled in CLARITY Extension, participation rates were 62% in the placebo group, 46% in the cladribine 3.5 mg/kg group, and 56% in the cladribine 5.25 mg/kg group. column37: Overall risk of bias was judged High. In the Extension, only participants from CLARITY were enrolled; those previously treated with cladribine were re-randomized (2:1) to cladribine 3.5 mg/kg or placebo via centralized IVRS, whereas prior-placebo participants were directly assigned to cladribine 3.5 mg/kg without re-randomization, creating five arms and undermining exchangeability across groups. Baseline comparability was further threatened by evidence of greater disease activity among prior-placebo entrants. Although the trial maintained double-blind conduct and MRI outcomes were acquired on consistent scanners and centrally assessed by blinded neuroradiologists, selection and attrition were substantial and differential (only 46–62% of CLARITY arms entered the Extension; ~7–11% did not complete), and Extension eligibility required normal hematologic parameters within 28 days—introducing prognostically related selection. The variable gap between CLARITY and the Extension and the limited Extension sample meant efficacy objectives were exploratory and the original treatment-versus-placebo contrasts could not be replicated. Taken together—partial/randomization, post-randomization selection, and incomplete follow-up—these features indicate a high overall risk of bias despite adequate blinding of outcome measurement.
